Other restrictive etiologies (e.g., idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, HP) lack supporting features (no dyspnea, no crackles, no systemic symptoms, no radiographic description) and do not explain the purulent sputum burden.  

Thus, while HRCT is urgently needed for confirmation, the pre-test probability of bronchiectasis is very high — and no other diagnosis better accounts for the totality of findings.

[EVIDENCE]  
- 11-year history of chronic productive cough with thick, foamy, yellow-green sputum  
- Recurrent antibiotic-treated bronchitis (>2–3 episodes/year for many years)  
- Absence of smoking history, atopy, wheeze, clubbing, or chronic sinus symptoms  
- Pulmonary function testing shows reduced FVC and FEV1 with normal FEV1/FVC ratio → restrictive ventilatory defect  
- Sputum culture shows heavy growth of non-specific bacteria  
- No evidence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis or fungal infection on sputum studies  
- Clinical summary explicitly identifies bronchiectasis as the most likely diagnosis pending HRCT  

[GAPS]  
- High-resolution chest CT (HRCT) — gold standard for diagnosing bronchiectasis; essential to confirm presence, pattern, and distribution  
- Serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM) and IgG subclasses — to assess for common variable immunodeficiency or selective IgG subclass deficiency  
- Alpha-1 antitrypsin level — to exclude A1AT deficiency, which can cause bronchiectasis and/or early-onset panacinar emphysema  
- Sweat chloride test and CFTR genetic testing — to rule out cystic fibrosis or CFTR-related disorders, especially in adults with atypical presentations  
- NTM-specific sputum studies (AFB culture, NTM PCR) — to exclude nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, which can mimic or coexist with bronchiectasis  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Bronchiectasis
